blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 26 (Polymers), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define polymer and monomer.
blocks.explanation: Polymers are very large molecules made by joining many small molecules through polymerisation. The small molecules that join to make the polymer are called monomers, e.g. ethene is the monomer of poly(ethene).

book_ref.quote: Polymers are very large molecules made by joining many small molecules called monomers through polymerisation.

blocks.prompt: 2 Give one example each of a very light, soft polymer and of a hard polymer, with a use of each.
blocks.explanation: Light and soft: poly(ethene), used for shopping bags (poly(propene) for clothesline is another). Hard and thermally stable: Kevlar®, used in bulletproof vests and aerospace applications.

book_ref.quote: Some polymers are very light and soft, which are suitable for applications where soft materials are needed.

blocks.prompt: 3 How are synthetic polymers named systematically? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: The prefix "poly" is written before the name of the monomer. Polythene is poly(ethene) and polyvinylchloride is poly(chloroethene).

book_ref.quote: Synthetic polymers are named systematically by writing the prefix

blocks.prompt: 4 Why is PETE usually called by its common name?
blocks.explanation: PETE is made from two monomers, and for such polymers the systematic name is too long: poly(ethane-1,2-diyl benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate). So the common name polyethylene terephthalate (PETE) is used.

book_ref.quote: For polymers with two or more monomers, common names are usually used because the systematic name is too long.

blocks.prompt: 5 What is polymerisation? Name its two main types.
blocks.explanation: Polymerisation is the process of joining monomers to form a polymer. Its two main types are addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.

book_ref.quote: Polymerisation is the process of joining monomers to form a polymer.

blocks.prompt: 6 Define addition polymerisation. Why is it said that 'nothing is lost' in it?
blocks.explanation: In addition polymerisation monomers add to each other one by one, forming long chains. All the atoms of the original monomers become part of the polymer and no small molecule such as water is produced, so nothing is lost.

book_ref.quote: In addition polymerization, monomers add to each other one by one, forming long chains.

blocks.prompt: 7 Why must a monomer for addition polymerisation contain a C=C or C≡C bond? How is the reaction usually started?
blocks.explanation: The multiple bond "opens up" and allows the monomers to link together. The reaction often happens as a chain reaction started by a very reactive molecule, an initiator, which forms free radicals.

book_ref.quote: This bond "opens up" to allow monomers to link together.

blocks.prompt: 8 Write the equation for the formation of poly(ethene) from ethene.
blocks.explanation: n CH₂=CH₂ → —[CH₂—CH₂]ₙ—. A large number of ethene molecules add together by breaking their double bonds and linking end-to-end.

book_ref.quote: Polyethene, a large number of ethene (CH₂=CH₂) molecules add together by breaking double bonds and linking end-to-end.

blocks.prompt: 9 Differentiate between LDPE and HDPE.
blocks.explanation: LDPE has more branched chains and is light, soft and elastic; HDPE has linear, closely packed chains and is tough and dense.

book_ref.quote: This makes it unable to pack tightly giving a less solid and more elastic material.

rows: Used where a very light, soft material is needed: shopping bags, light plastic bottles
Used for plastic containers, thick shopping bags, toys

blocks.prompt: 10 What is the importance of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst?
blocks.explanation: Discovered by Karl Ziegler in 1953, it enabled for the first time the low-pressure polymerisation of ethene into linear HDPE. Giulio Natta expanded it to make stereoregular polymers such as crystalline polypropylene; it is a Nobel Prize-winning invention.

book_ref.quote: This catalyst enabled, for the first time, the low-pressure polymerisation of ethene into linear, high-density poly(ethene) (HDPE).

blocks.prompt: 11 Write the equation for the formation of PVC.
blocks.explanation: n CH₂=CHCl → —[CH₂—CHCl]ₙ—. Chloroethene molecules join by addition polymerisation; the C=C bonds open and the units link end-to-end.

book_ref.quote: Poly(chloroethene) or PVC is made from a monomer called chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl) through an addition polymerisation reaction.

blocks.prompt: 12 Define plasticizers and state how they act.
blocks.explanation: Plasticizers are chemicals added to materials to make them softer, more flexible and easier to work with. They reduce the strong forces between polymer chains, allowing the chains to move more freely.

book_ref.quote: Plasticizers are chemicals added to materials to make them softer, more flexible, and easier to work with.

blocks.prompt: 13 Differentiate between rigid PVC and plasticised PVC.
blocks.explanation: Rigid PVC has no plasticizers and is hard and stiff; plasticised PVC contains plasticizers and is flexible and soft.

book_ref.quote: Plasticised PVC (with plasticisers) is flexible and soft, so it can be bent and shaped easily.

rows: Hard and stiff, does not bend easily
Flexible and soft, can be bent and shaped easily
Keeps good chemical and electrical properties

blocks.prompt: 14 Why is rigid PVC described as chemically inert and self-extinguishing?
blocks.explanation: It is chemically inert because it does not react with most acids, bases or oils. Due to its chlorine atoms it is naturally resistant to burning and self-extinguishing.

book_ref.quote: It is chemically inert because it does not react with most acids, bases, or oils.

blocks.prompt: 15 Why is PVC used for water supply, drainage and sewage pipes?
blocks.explanation: PVC resists corrosion and is durable; it is chemically inert to most acids, bases and oils, and lasts a long time and resists weathering.

book_ref.quote: Pipes and fittings for water supply, drainage, and sewage systems due to its corrosion resistance and durability.

blocks.prompt: 16 Define condensation polymerisation. Name the small molecules that may be eliminated.
blocks.explanation: In condensation polymerisation monomers join together, but each time a new bond forms a small molecule is eliminated. The molecule is usually water; it can also be HCl, CH₃OH or NH₃.

book_ref.quote: In condensation polymerisation, monomers join together, but each time a new bond forms, a small molecule is eliminated from the monomers.

blocks.prompt: 17 What structural feature must the monomers of condensation polymerisation have?
blocks.explanation: They must have at least two reactive functional groups (such as -OH, -COOH, -NH₂) that can react with each other, and these groups are on different ends of the monomer(s).

book_ref.quote: These groups are on different ends of the monomer(s).

blocks.prompt: 18 What are polyesters? Write the equation for the preparation of Terylene (PET).
blocks.explanation: Polyesters have ester links [—C(=O)—O—] in the backbone, made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid with loss of water. n HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH + n HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH → —[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ— + 2n H₂O.

book_ref.quote: A diol (molecule with two -OH groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (molecule with two -COOH groups) as monomers are combined to give polyester.

blocks.prompt: 19 Give three uses of polyesters.
blocks.explanation: (1) Fibres, due to high tensile strength, and as an alternative to cotton (low cost, crease resistant). (2) Plastic: PETE bottles for beverages and food packaging. (3) Cross links in hard plastics, e.g. glass fibre reinforced cross-linked polyester.

book_ref.quote: It is also used as a plastic; for example, PETE is used in making plastic bottles for beverages and other food packaging.

blocks.prompt: 20 What are polyamides? Name three types of starting materials for them.
blocks.explanation: Polyamides have amide links [—C(=O)—NH—] in their backbone. They can be made from (i) a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, (ii) a diamine and a dioyl chloride, (iii) amino acids.

book_ref.quote: Polyamides have amide links [—C(=O)—NH—] in their backbone. They can be prepared from many starting materials.

blocks.prompt: 21 Compare the preparation of a polyamide from a dicarboxylic acid and from a dioyl chloride.
blocks.explanation: Both react with a diamine to give amide links; the dioyl chloride is more reactive and gives HCl instead of water.

book_ref.quote: The -NH₂ from the diamine reacts with the -COCl from the dioyl chloride.

rows: Water is removed (2n H₂O for n repeat units)
HCl is removed (2n HCl for n repeat units)

blocks.prompt: 22 Why does the formation of n repeat units of a polyamide from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid release 2n H₂O, but n repeat units from an amino acid release only n H₂O?
blocks.explanation: Each link releases one water molecule. In the diamine-diacid polymer each repeat unit has two amide links, so 2n H₂O; in the amino-acid polymer each repeat unit has one link, so n H₂O.

book_ref.quote: Each repeat unit has two amide links and each link releases one small molecule

blocks.prompt: 23 What is a peptide bond? Why are proteins called natural polyamides?
blocks.explanation: When the -NH₂ group of one amino acid reacts with the -COOH group of another, water is removed and a peptide bond (-CO-NH-), a type of amide linkage, forms. Proteins are made from amino acids joined by such links, so they are natural polyamides.

book_ref.quote: The -NH₂ group of one amino acid reacts with the -COOH group of another amino acid removing a water to form a peptide bond.

blocks.prompt: 24 Write a general equation for the reaction of an acyl chloride with methanamine. Why does it take place at room temperature?
blocks.explanation: R–COCl + CH₃–NH₂ → R–CO–NH–CH₃ + HCl. An amide linkage forms and HCl gas is removed. It happens easily at room temperature because acyl chlorides are fairly reactive.

book_ref.quote: When an acyl chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine, a molecule of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas is removed.

blocks.prompt: 25 What is nylon? What are its general monomers?
blocks.explanation: Nylon is a synthetic polyamide formed by condensation polymerisation, usually from two different monomers: a diamine (H₂N-R-NH₂) and a dicarboxylic acid (HOOC-R-COOH). A small molecule, typically water, is removed.

book_ref.quote: Generally, a diamine (H₂N-R-NH₂) and a dicarboxylic acid (HOOC-R-COOH) act as monomers.

blocks.prompt: 26 Give the formula and the correct systematic name of adipic acid. Why is '1,4-hexanedioic acid' wrong?
blocks.explanation: Adipic acid is HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH. Its two COOH carbons are C1 and C6 of a six-carbon chain, so it is hexanedioic acid (hexane-1,6-dioic acid), not 1,4-.

book_ref.quote: Adipic acid, HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH, has its two COOH carbons at C1 and C6

blocks.prompt: 27 Why is the formation of nylon-6 not a typical condensation reaction, yet nylon-6 is a condensation polymer?
blocks.explanation: Nylon-6 forms from the single cyclic monomer caprolactam and no small molecule is removed, so it is not a typical condensation. It is still classified as a condensation polymer due to the mode of formation of its amide linkage.

book_ref.quote: Another type of nylon is nylon-6, which is formed from a single monomer called caprolactam as in the following scheme.

blocks.prompt: 28 Differentiate between nylon-6 and nylon-6,6.
blocks.explanation: Nylon-6 comes from one monomer, caprolactam, without loss of a small molecule; nylon-6,6 comes from two monomers with loss of water.

book_ref.quote: Nylon 6 is a harder material than nylon-6,6 and provides a smoother surface and higher impact resistance

rows: Single monomer: caprolactam (cyclic, six carbon atoms)
Lower melting point, easier to mold
Used in rollers, skateboard wheels, power tool handles

blocks.prompt: 29 Why are skateboard wheels made from nylon?
blocks.explanation: Because nylon is hard, smooth and shock-free. Nylon-6 in particular provides a smoother surface and higher impact resistance, so it is used in skateboard wheels and rollers to avoid shocks.

book_ref.quote: The wheels of this skateboard are made from nylon, due to its hard, smooth, and shock-free nature.

blocks.prompt: 30 List the properties of nylon.
blocks.explanation: Nylon is strong and resistant to breaking, withstands rubbing and wear and tear; stretchable due to elasticity; has a slippery surface that reduces friction; is resistant to oils, many solvents and alkalis; and has a high melting point.

book_ref.quote: Strong and resistant to breaking and can withstand rubbing and wear and tear.

blocks.prompt: 31 Why is nylon used for gears and bearings in the automotive industry?
blocks.explanation: Because of its strength, low friction (slippery surface) and heat resistance (high melting point). The same strength and wear resistance make it suitable for screws, nuts and bolts.

book_ref.quote: Nylon is used for the manufacturing of mechanical parts of automotive industry like gears, bearings, bushings, engine covers, and fuel lines

blocks.prompt: 32 Why is nylon used for clothing such as activewear and swimwear?
blocks.explanation: Nylon is strong and elastic (stretchable), so it is used for stockings, activewear, swimwear and carpets; its fabric is also used for raincoats and sportswear.

book_ref.quote: It is used for clothing (stockings, activewear, and swimwear), carpets, and ropes due to its strength and elasticity.

blocks.text: 26.3 Identifying the Type, Repeat Unit and Monomers of a Polymer

blocks.prompt: 33 How can you decide from the backbone whether a polymer is an addition or a condensation polymer?
blocks.explanation: Check the atoms of the main chain. If it contains only carbon atoms (-C-C-C-C-), it is an addition polymer formed from alkenes. If it contains O or N atoms along with carbon, it is a condensation polymer (polyester or polyamide).

book_ref.quote: The first thing to check is what atoms make up the main horizontal chain of the polymer

blocks.prompt: 34 How do you tell a polyester from a polyamide by its functional linkage?
blocks.explanation: If a carbonyl group (C=O) is directly attached next to an O, it is an ester linkage: a polyester (e.g. PET). If C=O is directly next to an N carrying an H, it is an amide (peptide) linkage: a polyamide (e.g. nylon-6,6, Kevlar).

book_ref.quote: Now, identify the functional linkage. There are again two possibilities:

blocks.prompt: 35 What is a repeat unit? How is it shown?
blocks.explanation: The repeat unit is the smallest section that repeats itself in the polymer. Look where the sequence starts to duplicate, place brackets around one recurring section and add the subscript n.

book_ref.quote: 2. Determining the Repeat Unit: To find the original monomers, one must first identify the smallest section that repeats itself in the section of the polymer.

blocks.prompt: 36 Identify the repeat unit and the monomer of the addition polymer section -CH₂-CH(C₆H₅)-CH₂-CH(C₆H₅)-CH₂-CH(C₆H₅)-.
blocks.explanation: Repeat unit: —[CH₂—CH(C₆H₅)]ₙ—. Changing the C-C single bond back into C=C gives the monomer CH₂=CH-C₆H₅, phenyl ethene (styrene).

book_ref.quote: a) For addition polymers, change the C-C single bond in the repeat unit back into a C=C double bond to find the monomer.

blocks.prompt: 37 How are the monomers of a condensation polymer found from its repeat unit? Apply it to the ester link -CO-O-.
blocks.explanation: Add water back: break the ester or amide bond, add -OH to the C=O side and -H to the O or N side. For -CO-O-, the C=O side becomes -COOH (acid) and the O side becomes -OH (alcohol).

book_ref.quote: b) For Condensation polymers: Add water back in. Break the ester or amide bond.

blocks.prompt: 38 Classify the following by Table 26.1: PTFE, PLA, nylon-6,6, PVC.
blocks.explanation: PTFE (poly(tetrafluoroethene)) and PVC: addition polymers (only C-C bonds in the chain). PLA: polyester (-COO- links). Nylon-6,6: polyamide (-CONH- links).

book_ref.quote: Poly(ethene), PVC, PTFE (poly (tetrafluoroethene))

blocks.prompt: 39 Why is Kevlar placed both among polyamides and among aromatic polymers in Table 26.1?
blocks.explanation: Kevlar has -CONH- (amide) links, so it is a polyamide; its chain also contains benzene rings, so it is an aromatic polymer as well.

book_ref.quote: Benzene rings in the chain

blocks.prompt: 40 Predict the type of polymerisation for ethene, propene and phenyl ethene. Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: All three undergo addition polymerisation, because each monomer contains a C=C bond.

book_ref.quote: When the given monomer(s) contains C=C bonds, addition polymerisation will take place.

blocks.prompt: 41 Differentiate between a homopolymer and a copolymer formed by addition polymerisation.
blocks.explanation: A homopolymer comes from one kind of monomer; a copolymer from two different monomers having double bonds.

book_ref.quote: sometimes copolymerisation of two different monomers having double bond can also be achieved

rows: One kind of monomer with C=C
Two different monomers, each with a double bond
e.g. copolymer of ethene and propenoic acid (H₂C=CH-COOH)

blocks.prompt: 42 Name the four pairs of functional groups that undergo condensation polymerisation, with the polymer and small molecule formed by each.
blocks.explanation: (1) NH₂ + COOH → polyamide + H₂O. (2) NH₂ + COCl → polyamide + HCl. (3) COOH + OH → polyester + H₂O. (4) COCl + OH → polyester + HCl.

book_ref.quote: The common functional groups that can undergo condensation polymerisation are:

blocks.prompt: 43 Predict the polymer formed from HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH and ClOC–C₆H₄–COCl and name the small molecule eliminated.
blocks.explanation: OH groups react with COCl groups, so a polyester forms by condensation and HCl is eliminated: n HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH + n ClOC–C₆H₄–COCl → —[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ— + 2n HCl.

book_ref.quote: acyl chlorides (COCl) and alcohols (OH) (polyester and HCl).

blocks.prompt: 44 How can lactic acid alone form a condensation polymer? Name the polymer.
blocks.explanation: Both functional groups needed (-OH and -COOH) are present in the single lactic acid molecule, so its molecules join to each other by ester links. The polymer is poly(lactic acid), PLA, a polyester.

book_ref.quote: The two functional group may exist in a single molecule (e.g. lactic acid) or two different molecules, as in the case of nylon 6,6.

blocks.prompt: 45 What are non-degradable polymers? Why are they an environmental nuisance?
blocks.explanation: Conventional polymers such as poly(ethene) are non-degradable: they cannot be broken down into simpler, non-toxic compounds. So after disposal they persist and become part of water bodies, soil and natural habitats of living organisms.

book_ref.quote: Non-degradable means that these polymers cannot be broken down into simpler, non-toxic compounds

blocks.prompt: 46 What are microplastics? How can they harm humans?
blocks.explanation: Microplastics are tiny pieces formed when large pieces of non-degradable plastics break down over time. They spread everywhere, polluting soil, water and air, and can enter the food chain and potentially harm human health.

book_ref.quote: These microplastics spread everywhere, polluting soil, water, and even the air.

blocks.prompt: 47 Define biodegradable plastic. Why do starch-containing plastics degrade faster?
blocks.explanation: Biodegradable plastic is naturally decomposed by microorganisms into simpler non-toxic compounds when buried for a certain period. Starch is a natural polymer, and soil bacteria attack natural polymers easily, so such plastics degrade faster.

book_ref.quote: The plastic that is naturally decomposed by microorganism into simpler non-toxic compounds when buried for a certain period is called biodegradable plastic.

blocks.prompt: 48 What are photodegradable polymers? Why are carbonyl groups built into some of them?
blocks.explanation: Photodegradable polymers have functional groups that absorb more energy from sunlight (UV) and so are degraded by light. Carbonyl groups (C=O) are built into chains for enhanced photoabsorption; the absorbed UV light weakens the bonds in the chain and the forces between chains.

book_ref.quote: Polymers with such functionalities can be degraded by light and are termed as photodegradable.

blocks.prompt: 49 State three limitations of photodegradable plastics.
blocks.explanation: (1) They cannot be used for a long time. (2) Their recycling is not efficient. (3) Plastic is buried in landfills where no light is available for photodegradation.

book_ref.quote: However, photodegradable plastics cannot be used for longer time and recycling of such polymers is not efficient.

blocks.prompt: 50 How is the slow hydrolysis of polyesters used in medicine?
blocks.explanation: Materials can be designed to break down when no longer needed. Some medical implants and dissolvable stitches are made from polyesters that slowly break down in the body through hydrolysis.

book_ref.quote: Scientists and engineers can use this knowledge to design materials that break down when they are no longer needed.

blocks.prompt: 51 What are artificial organs? List the requirements of polymers used in them.
blocks.explanation: Artificial organs are man-made devices that replace or support the function of damaged or diseased body parts. Their polymers must be biocompatible, mechanically suitable, sterilizable, durable and tunable.

book_ref.quote: Polymers used in the body need to be biocompatible, mechanically suitable, sterilizable, durable and tunable.

blocks.prompt: 52 Explain the terms biocompatible and tunable for polymers in artificial organs.
blocks.explanation: Biocompatible: the polymer must not harm the body, cause allergies, or be rejected by the immune system. Tunable: its strength, flexibility or elasticity can be adjusted to match the body part, e.g. flexible for blood vessels, strong for bones.

book_ref.quote: flexible for blood vessels, strong for bones

blocks.prompt: 53 Which polymers are used for artificial blood vessels, and why?
blocks.explanation: PTFE (poly(tetrafluoroethylene)) and PET (poly(ethylene terephthalate)). They give smooth surfaces that prevent blood clots, and are used to replace or bypass blocked vessels.

book_ref.quote: Smooth surfaces to prevent blood clots; used to replace or bypass blocked vessels.

blocks.prompt: 54 Name the polymers used for an artificial cornea and state the properties they must have.
blocks.explanation: Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) and hydrogels. They must be perfectly clear (transparent) and biocompatible to restore vision.

book_ref.quote: Must be perfectly clear (transparent) and biocompatible to restore vision.

blocks.prompt: 55 Why is UHMWPE used in artificial hip and knee joints?
blocks.explanation: Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene provides a smooth, low-friction surface that allows movement and resists wear.

book_ref.quote: Provides a smooth, low-friction surface to allow movement and resist wear.
